General Duties of Businesses that Collect Personal Information
Notice of categories and purposes at/before collection

At or before the point of collection, disclose to consumers: (1) the categories of personal information (PI) to be collected; (2) the purposes for which PI is collected or used; (3) whether that PI is sold or shared. A business shall not collect additional categories of PI or use PI for additional purposes incompatible with the disclosed purpose without providing updated notice consistent with this section.
All three thresholds (revenue >$25M; 100K+ consumers; 50%+ revenue from PI sale)
Privacy notice / collection notice; data inventory/mapping records; DPA/contract templates with third parties; data minimization policy; security assessment
General Duties of Businesses that Collect Personal Information
Notice of sensitive personal information (SPI) categories and purposes

At or before the point of collection, disclose: (1) the categories of sensitive personal information (SPI) to be collected; (2) purposes for which SPI is collected or used; (3) whether SPI is sold or shared. A business shall not collect additional SPI categories or use SPI for additional purposes incompatible with the disclosed purpose without providing updated notice.
All three thresholds (revenue >$25M; 100K+ consumers; 50%+ revenue from PI sale)
Privacy notice / collection notice; data inventory/mapping records; DPA/contract templates with third parties; data minimization policy; security assessment
General Duties of Businesses that Collect Personal Information

Disclose the length of time the business intends to retain each category of PI and SPI, or if not possible, the criteria used to determine that period. A business shall not retain consumer PI or SPI for each disclosed purpose for longer than is reasonably necessary for that disclosed purpose.
All three thresholds (revenue >$25M; 100K+ consumers; 50%+ revenue from PI sale)
Privacy notice / collection notice; data inventory/mapping records; DPA/contract templates with third parties; data minimization policy; security assessment
General Duties of Businesses that Collect Personal Information

A business acting as a third party controlling collection of PI may satisfy notice obligations by posting required information prominently and conspicuously on its website homepage. If collecting PI on-premises (including in a vehicle), the business must inform consumers of PI categories collected, purposes, and whether PI is sold at the collection location in a clear and conspicuous manner.
All three thresholds (revenue >$25M; 100K+ consumers; 50%+ revenue from PI sale)
Privacy notice / collection notice; data inventory/mapping records; DPA/contract templates with third parties; data minimization policy; security assessment
General Duties of Businesses that Collect Personal Information

A business's collection, use, retention, and sharing of consumer PI shall be reasonably necessary and proportionate to achieve the purposes for which PI was collected or processed, or for another disclosed purpose compatible with the collection context. PI must not be further processed in a manner incompatible with those purposes.
All three thresholds (revenue >$25M; 100K+ consumers; 50%+ revenue from PI sale)
Privacy notice / collection notice; data inventory/mapping records; DPA/contract templates with third parties; data minimization policy; security assessment
General Duties of Businesses that Collect Personal Information
Contractual obligations with third parties, service providers & contractors

When selling or sharing PI with a third party, or disclosing to a service provider/contractor, the business must enter a written agreement that: (1) specifies PI is disclosed only for limited and specified purposes; (2) obligates the recipient to comply with CCPA obligations; (3) grants the business rights to ensure compliant PI use; (4) requires recipient to notify if it can no longer meet obligations; (5) grants the business the right to stop and remediate unauthorized PI use upon notice.
All three thresholds (revenue >$25M; 100K+ consumers; 50%+ revenue from PI sale)
Privacy notice / collection notice; data inventory/mapping records; DPA/contract templates with third parties; data minimization policy; security assessment
General Duties of Businesses that Collect Personal Information

A business that collects consumer PI shall implement reasonable security procedures and practices appropriate to the nature of the PI to protect it from unauthorized or illegal access, destruction, use, modification, or disclosure in accordance with Civil Code § 1798.81.5.
All three thresholds (revenue >$25M; 100K+ consumers; 50%+ revenue from PI sale)
Privacy notice / collection notice; data inventory/mapping records; DPA/contract templates with third parties; data minimization policy; security assessment
General Duties of Businesses that Collect Personal Information

Nothing in § 1798.100 shall require a business to disclose trade secrets, as specified in regulations adopted pursuant to § 1798.185(a)(3). Businesses may withhold information that qualifies as a trade secret when responding to consumer requests.
All three thresholds (revenue >$25M; 100K+ consumers; 50%+ revenue from PI sale)
Privacy notice / collection notice; data inventory/mapping records; DPA/contract templates with third parties; data minimization policy; security assessment

A consumer shall have the right to request that a business delete any personal information about the consumer which the business has collected from the consumer. This right applies to all PI collected regardless of the channel or method of collection.

Deletion and downstream notification upon verifiable request

Upon receiving a verifiable consumer request (VCR): (1) delete the consumer's PI from its records; (2) notify any service providers or contractors to delete the consumer's PI from their records; (3) notify all third parties to whom the business has sold or shared the PI to delete it — unless this proves impossible or involves disproportionate effort.

sheets.name: 📖 How to Use
detected_headers:
CMMI is a
Performance
Improvement
Model

CMMI (Capability Maturity Model Integration) is a process improvement framework — not a technical compliance standard or a cybersecurity control framework. ISACA, which now stewards CMMI, describes it as a model for improving organisational performance and capability maturity across people, processes, and technology.

It is fundamentally different from frameworks such as ISO 27001, NIST CSF, SOC 2, or PCI-DSS, which prescribe specific controls and are used for external audit and certification. CMMI instead describes how well an organisation's processes are defined, managed, measured, and optimised — and uses appraisals (not audits) to assess that maturity.

Key implication for GRC teams: Do NOT treat this checklist as a list of controls to tick off. Instead, use it to evaluate process capability and identify improvement opportunities.

sheets.name: DPDPA Act Sections
detected_headers: Processing personal data is permissible only on two grounds: (1) consent of the Data Principal; or (2) certain legitimate uses as specified in section 7 of the Act.
preview_rows: Processing personal data is permissible only on two grounds: (1) consent of the Data Principal; or (2) certain legitimate uses as specified in section 7 of the Act.

Before or at the time of collecting personal data, the Data Fiduciary must give the Data Principal a notice containing details of the personal data to be collected, the purpose of processing, and the manner in which she may exercise her rights and make complaints. Rule 3 operationalises this.

Consent must be free, specific, informed, unconditional and unambiguous with a clear affirmative action. It must be limited to the specified purpose. The Data Principal may withdraw consent at any time. The Data Fiduciary must provide means to withdraw with ease comparable to giving consent.

Personal data may be processed without consent for: (a) State functions; (b) compliance with law; (c) medical emergency; (d) epidemic/public health; (e) employment; (f) court orders; (g) safety of Data Principal; (h) other notified purposes. Rule 5 and Second Schedule operationalise sub-clause (b).

Data Fiduciary obligations include: processing only for specified purpose; ensuring accuracy and completeness; implementing security safeguards (Rule 6); notifying breaches (Rule 7); erasing data when purpose is served (Rule 8); contracts with Data Processors; and appointing a Data Protection Officer (for Significant Data Fiduciaries).
Processing of personal data of children

Before processing any personal data of a child (under 18), the Data Fiduciary must obtain verifiable consent of the parent (Rules 10–12 operationalise this). It must not undertake tracking, behavioural monitoring, or targeted advertising directed at children.

Significant Data Fiduciaries (notified by Central Government based on volume, sensitivity, risk) must: appoint a Data Protection Officer (Indian resident); appoint an independent data auditor; undertake DPIA and audit (Rule 13); and comply with other prescribed obligations.
Rights and Duties of Data Principal

A Data Principal may request from the Data Fiduciary: (a) a summary of the personal data processed; (b) identities of all Data Fiduciaries and Data Processors with whom data is shared; and (c) any other information prescribed. Rule 14 operationalises this.
Rights and Duties of Data Principal

A Data Principal may request the Data Fiduciary to: correct inaccurate or misleading personal data; complete incomplete data; update data; and erase personal data that is no longer necessary for the specified purpose or for which consent has been withdrawn. Rule 14 operationalises this.

preview_rows: GDPR COMPLIANCE CONTROLS & SUB-CONTROLS REFERENCE  |  Regulation (EU) 2016/679
Sets out the seven foundational principles that must govern all processing of personal data.
Personal data must be processed lawfully, fairly and in a transparent manner in relation to the data subject.
Data must be collected for specified, explicit and legitimate purposes and not further processed in an incompatible manner.
Data must be adequate, relevant and limited to what is necessary in relation to the purposes for which it is processed.
Data must be accurate and kept up to date; inaccurate data must be erased or rectified without delay.
Data must be kept in identifiable form only as long as necessary for the processing purpose.
Data must be processed with appropriate security, including protection against unauthorised access and accidental loss or destruction.
The controller is responsible for, and must be able to demonstrate, compliance with all the above principles.
Lists the six lawful bases on which personal data may be processed.
Processing is lawful where the data subject has given consent for one or more specific purposes.

sheets.name: Ch III
preview_rows: GDPR COMPLIANCE CONTROLS & SUB-CONTROLS REFERENCE  |  Regulation (EU) 2016/679
Governs how controllers must communicate with data subjects — setting standards for clarity, timing, format, and charges for responding to rights requests.
Concise, transparent, intelligible, easily accessible form
All information provided to data subjects must be concise, transparent, intelligible and easily accessible.
Clear and plain language (especially for children)
Information must be provided using clear and plain language, with particular attention to child-directed communication.
Written, electronic or oral provision of information
Information may be provided in writing, electronically, or orally (with identity verified by other means) on request.
Response within one month (extendable by 2 months)
Controllers must respond to data subject requests within one month; complex or numerous requests may extend this by a further two months with notification.
Responses to data subject requests are free of charge unless requests are manifestly unfounded or excessive, in which case a fee may be charged or the request refused.
Identity verification where reasonable doubt exists
Where there is reasonable doubt about the requester's identity, the controller may request additional information to confirm identity.
Information may be presented alongside standardised icons to give a meaningful overview of intended processing in a visible, legible manner.
The Commission is empowered to adopt delegated acts determining what information the icons present and the procedures for providing them.

sheets.name: Ch IV
preview_rows: GDPR COMPLIANCE CONTROLS & SUB-CONTROLS REFERENCE  |  Regulation (EU) 2016/679
Establishes the accountability principle — requiring controllers to implement appropriate measures and demonstrate compliance with GDPR.
Implement appropriate technical and organisational measures
Controllers must implement measures appropriate to the nature, scope, context, purposes of processing and risk to data subjects' rights.
Controllers must be able to demonstrate that processing is performed in accordance with the Regulation — the 'accountability' requirement.
Measures must be reviewed and updated where necessary to remain effective.
Implement data protection policies proportionate to processing
Where proportionate, controllers must implement appropriate data protection policies.
Codes of conduct / certification as evidence of compliance
Adherence to approved codes of conduct or certification mechanisms may be used as an element demonstrating controller compliance.
Data protection by design and by default
Requires controllers to embed data protection into systems and processes from the design stage and to process only minimum necessary data by default.
Implement data-protection principles (e.g. pseudonymisation, minimisation) at design stage
At the time of determining processing means and at time of processing itself, controllers must implement appropriate technical and organisational measures to implement data-protection principles.
Data protection by design and by default
By default: process only necessary data for each purpose
By default, only personal data necessary for each specific purpose should be processed, including limiting data collected, extent of processing, storage period, and accessibility.
Data protection by design and by default
Controls on amount, extent, storage period, and accessibility
The default measures must ensure that personal data are not made accessible to an indefinite number of persons without individual intervention.

sheets.name: Ch V
preview_rows: GDPR COMPLIANCE CONTROLS & SUB-CONTROLS REFERENCE  |  Regulation (EU) 2016/679
Establishes the fundamental principle that transfers of personal data to third countries must comply with all Chapter V conditions.
Transfers only if conditions in Chapter V are complied with
Any transfer to a third country or international organisation is only permitted if the conditions in Chapter V are fully complied with.
All provisions applied to ensure EU protection level not undermined
All Chapter V provisions must be applied to ensure that the level of protection guaranteed by GDPR is not undermined.
Applies to onward transfers from third countries
The requirement applies to all transfers including onward transfers of personal data from the third country or international organisation.
Permits transfers to third countries where the Commission has determined that the country provides an adequate level of data protection.
Transfer without specific authorisation where Commission adequacy decision exists
Where the Commission has adopted an adequacy decision, transfers to that third country may take place without any specific authorisation.
Commission considers: rule of law, human rights, effective supervisory authorities, international commitments
In assessing adequacy, the Commission evaluates these specific factors.
Implementing act with periodic review (at least every 4 years)
Adequacy decisions must include a mechanism for periodic review at least every four years.
Commission monitors developments in third countries
The Commission shall on an ongoing basis monitor developments in third countries that could affect functioning of adequacy decisions.
Where a third country no longer ensures adequate protection, the Commission must repeal, amend or suspend the decision.

sheets.name: Ch VI
preview_rows: GDPR COMPLIANCE CONTROLS & SUB-CONTROLS REFERENCE  |  Regulation (EU) 2016/679
Requires each Member State to establish at least one independent supervisory authority.
Each Member State establishes one or more independent public authorities
Each Member State must provide for one or more independent public authorities responsible for monitoring GDPR application and protecting data subjects' rights.
Supervisory authorities contribute to consistent application of GDPR
Each supervisory authority must contribute to the consistent application of GDPR throughout the EU by cooperating with other supervisory authorities and the Commission.
Multi-authority states designate representative for the Board
Where a Member State has more than one supervisory authority, it must designate one to represent all in the Board.
Notify Commission of law provisions by 25 May 2018
Each Member State shall notify to the Commission the provisions of its law adopted pursuant to this Chapter by 25 May 2018 and any subsequent amendment.
Guarantees the full independence of supervisory authorities from external influence.
Each supervisory authority must act with complete independence in performing its tasks and exercising its powers.
Free from external influence (direct or indirect)
Members of supervisory authorities must remain free from external influence and must neither seek nor take instructions from any person.
In the performance of their tasks and exercise of their powers, members must neither seek nor take instructions from anybody.
No incompatible occupations during term of office
Members must refrain from any action incompatible with their duties and must not engage in incompatible occupations during their term.

sheets.name: Ch VII
preview_rows: GDPR COMPLIANCE CONTROLS & SUB-CONTROLS REFERENCE  |  Regulation (EU) 2016/679
Cooperation between lead and other supervisory authorities
Establishes the cooperation procedure between the lead supervisory authority and other concerned supervisory authorities for cross-border cases.
Lead authority cooperates with concerned authorities to reach consensus
The lead supervisory authority must cooperate with concerned authorities in an endeavour to reach consensus, exchanging all relevant information.
Cooperation between lead and other supervisory authorities
The lead supervisory authority and the supervisory authorities concerned shall exchange all relevant information with each other.
Cooperation between lead and other supervisory authorities
Lead authority may request mutual assistance and joint operations
The lead supervisory authority may request at any time other supervisory authorities concerned to provide mutual assistance and may conduct joint operations.
Cooperation between lead and other supervisory authorities
Lead authority communicates information and submits draft decision for opinions
The lead authority must submit a draft decision to concerned authorities for their opinion; concerned authorities may raise relevant and reasoned objections within four weeks.
Cooperation between lead and other supervisory authorities
Concerned authority may raise relevant and reasoned objection within 4 weeks
Where any concerned supervisory authority raises a relevant and reasoned objection, the lead authority must decide whether to follow it or submit the matter to the Board.
Cooperation between lead and other supervisory authorities
Objection leads to consistency mechanism if not followed
If the lead authority does not follow a relevant and reasoned objection, the matter must be submitted to the Board consistency mechanism.
Cooperation between lead and other supervisory authorities
Revised draft decision subject to 2-week opinion period
Where the lead supervisory authority intends to follow the relevant and reasoned objection made, it shall submit a revised draft decision for opinion within two weeks.
Cooperation between lead and other supervisory authorities
Deemed agreement if no objection within period

Where none of the other supervisory authorities concerned has objected to the draft decision within the specified period, the lead authority and concerned authorities shall be deemed to be in agreement.

sheets.name: Ch VIII
preview_rows: GDPR COMPLIANCE CONTROLS & SUB-CONTROLS REFERENCE  |  Regulation (EU) 2016/679
Right to lodge complaint with supervisory authority
Grants every data subject the right to lodge a complaint with a supervisory authority.
Every data subject may lodge complaint in Member State of habitual residence, work, or alleged infringement
Every data subject has the right to lodge a complaint with a supervisory authority in the Member State of habitual residence, place of work, or place of the alleged infringement.
Right to lodge complaint with supervisory authority
Supervisory authority informs complainant of progress and outcome including judicial remedy possibility
The supervisory authority must inform the complainant of the progress and outcome of the complaint, including the possibility of a judicial remedy.
Right to judicial remedy against supervisory authority
Grants natural and legal persons the right to seek judicial remedy against legally binding supervisory authority decisions or inaction on complaints.
Judicial remedy against legally binding supervisory authority decision
Every natural or legal person has the right to an effective judicial remedy against a legally binding decision of a supervisory authority concerning them.
Right to judicial remedy against supervisory authority
Remedy where supervisory authority does not handle complaint or fails to inform within 3 months
Data subjects have a right to judicial remedy where the supervisory authority does not handle a complaint or fails to inform the data subject within three months of progress or outcome.
Right to judicial remedy against supervisory authority
Proceedings before courts of Member State where supervisory authority is established
Proceedings against a supervisory authority must be brought before the courts of the Member State where that authority is established.
Right to judicial remedy against supervisory authority
Court must receive Board opinion or decision used in the case

Where proceedings are brought against a decision of a supervisory authority preceded by an opinion or decision of the Board, the supervisory authority shall forward that opinion or decision to the court.
Right to judicial remedy against controller or processor
Grants data subjects the right to seek an effective judicial remedy against a controller or processor where their rights have been infringed.
Judicial remedy where rights infringed by non-compliant processing
Data subjects have the right to an effective judicial remedy where their GDPR rights have been infringed as a result of non-compliant processing of their personal data.
Right to judicial remedy against controller or processor
Proceedings in Member State of controller/processor establishment
Proceedings against a controller or a processor shall be brought before the courts of the Member State where the controller or processor has an establishment.

sheets.name: Ch IX
preview_rows: GDPR COMPLIANCE CONTROLS & SUB-CONTROLS REFERENCE  |  Regulation (EU) 2016/679
Requires Member States to reconcile data protection rights with freedom of expression and information.
Member States reconcile data protection with freedom of expression/information
Member States must by law reconcile the right to data protection with the right to freedom of expression and information, including journalistic, academic, artistic and literary expression.
Exemptions for journalistic, academic, artistic, literary purposes may be provided from: Chapters II, III, IV, V, VI, VII, IX
For journalistic and artistic/literary purposes, Member States may provide exemptions from these Chapters where necessary to balance the two fundamental rights.
Law of controller's Member State applies where exemptions differ
Where such exemptions or derogations differ from one Member State to another, the law of the Member State to which the controller is subject should apply.

45 CFR Part 160 & Part 164, Subparts A and C  |  Centers for Medicare & Medicaid Services (CMS)

The Security Rule (45 CFR Part 160 and Part 164, Subparts A and C) establishes national standards for protecting electronic protected health information (EPHI). It was adopted under the Health Insurance Portability and Accountability Act of 1996 (HIPAA) to implement security safeguards for all covered entities that handle EPHI.

CONFIDENTIALITY – Ensure EPHI is accessible only by authorized people and processes.
INTEGRITY – Ensure EPHI is not altered or destroyed in an unauthorized manner.
AVAILABILITY – Ensure EPHI can be accessed as needed by authorized persons.

1. Covered Health Care Providers – Providers transmitting health information electronically.
2. Health Plans – Individual or group plans providing/paying for health care.
3. Health Care Clearinghouses – Entities processing health care transactions.
4. Business Associates – Organizations handling EPHI on behalf of covered entities.

April 20, 2005 – All covered entities except small health plans.
April 20, 2006 – Small health plans.
Note: Security is an ongoing, dynamic process — not a one-time project.

Privacy Rule: Applies to ALL forms of PHI (electronic, written, oral). Enforced by OCR/HHS.
Security Rule: Applies ONLY to electronic PHI (EPHI). Enforced by CMS.
Entities compliant with Privacy Rule safeguards may already satisfy some Security Rule requirements.

REQUIRED (R) – Must be implemented; covered entity must implement policies/procedures as specified.
ADDRESSABLE (A) – Must be assessed for reasonableness. If not implemented, entity must document rationale and implement an equivalent alternative. 'Addressable' does NOT mean optional.

The information security management program (ISMP) has been established, implemented, operational, monitored, reviewed, and maintained. The ISMP is formally documented, protected, controlled, and retained according to federal, state and organizational requirements. The ISMP also incorporates a Plan, Do, Check, Act (PDCA) cycle for continuous improvement in the ISMP, particularly as information is obtained that could improve the ISMP, or indicates any shortcomings of the ISMP.

The information security management program (ISMP) has appropriate resources, roles, and responsibilities defined to establish, implement, operate, monitor, review, and maintain the ISMP. Further, independent audits also determine the continuing suitability, adequacy and effectiveness of the program. The organization continuously improves the ISMP through the use of the information security policy, information security objectives, audit results, analysis of monitored events, corrective and preventative actions and management review. The above requirements are to be formally defined and documented in the policies and/or standards.

PII controllers revise their notices to reflect any changes in their practices, policies or activities that affect PII, before or as soon as practicable after the change. preview_rows:
a. Develop, document, and disseminate to [Assignment: organization-defined personnel or roles]:
1. [Selection (one or more): organization-level; mission/business process-level; system-level] access control policy that:
(a) Addresses purpose, scope, roles, responsibilities, management commitment, coordination among organizational entities, and compliance; and
(b) Is consistent with applicable laws, executive orders, directives, regulations, policies, standards, and guidelines; and
2. Procedures to facilitate the implementation of the access control policy and the associated access controls;
b. Designate an [Assignment: organization-defined official] to manage the development, documentation, and dissemination of the access control policy and procedures; and
c. Review and update the current access control:
1. Policy [Assignment: organization-defined frequency] and following [Assignment: organization-defined events]; and
2. Procedures [Assignment: organization-defined frequency] and following [Assignment: organization-defined events].

Access control policy and procedures address the controls in the AC family that are implemented within systems and organizations. The risk management strategy is an important factor in establishing such policies and procedures. Policies and procedures contribute to security and privacy assurance. Therefore, it is important that security and privacy programs collaborate on the development of access control policy and procedures. Security and privacy program policies and procedures at the organization level are preferable, in general, and may obviate the need for mission- or system-specific policies and procedures. The policy can be included as part of the general security and privacy policy or be represented by multiple policies reflecting the complex nature of organizations. Procedures can be established for security and privacy programs, for mission or business processes, and for systems, if needed. Procedures describe how the policies or controls are implemented and can be directed at the individual or role that is the object of the procedure. Procedures can be documented in system security and privacy plans or in one or more separate documents. Events that may precipitate an update to access control policy and procedures include assessment or audit findings, security or privacy incidents, or changes in laws, executive orders, directives, regulations, policies, standards, and guidelines. Simply restating controls does not constitute an organizational policy or procedure.

Examples of system account types include individual, shared, group, system, guest, anonymous, emergency, developer, temporary, and service. Identification of authorized system users and the specification of access privileges reflect the requirements in other controls in the security plan. Users requiring administrative privileges on system accounts receive additional scrutiny by organizational personnel responsible for approving such accounts and privileged access, including system owner, mission or business owner, senior agency information security officer, or senior agency official for privacy. Types of accounts that organizations may wish to prohibit due to increased risk include shared, group, emergency, anonymous, temporary, and guest accounts.
Where access involves personally identifiable information, security programs collaborate with the senior agency official for privacy to establish the specific conditions for group and role membership; specify authorized users, group and role membership, and access authorizations for each account; and create, adjust, or remove system accounts in accordance with organizational policies. Policies can include such information as account expiration dates or other factors that trigger the disabling of accounts. Organizations may choose to define access privileges or other attributes by account, type of account, or a combination of the two. Examples of other attributes required for authorizing access include restrictions on time of day, day of week, and point of origin. In defining other system account attributes, organizations consider system-related requirements and mission/business requirements. Failure to consider these factors could affect system availability.
Temporary and emergency accounts are intended for short-term use. Organizations establish temporary accounts as part of normal account activation procedures when there is a need for short-term accounts without the demand for immediacy in account activation. Organizations establish emergency accounts in response to crisis situations and with the need for rapid account activation. Therefore, emergency account activation may bypass normal account authorization processes. Emergency and temporary accounts are not to be confused with infrequently used accounts, including local logon accounts used for special tasks or when network resources are unavailable (may also be known as accounts of last resort). Such accounts remain available and are not subject to automatic disabling or removal dates. Conditions for disabling or deactivating accounts include when shared/group, emergency, or temporary accounts are no longer required and when individuals are transferred or terminated. Changing shared/group authenticators when members leave the group is intended to ensure that former group members do not retain access to the shared or group account. Some types of system accounts may require specialized training.
Account Management | Automated System Account Management
Support the management of system accounts using [Assignment: organization-defined automated mechanisms].

Automated system account management includes using automated mechanisms to create, enable, modify, disable, and remove accounts; notify account managers when an account is created, enabled, modified, disabled, or removed, or when users are terminated or transferred; monitor system account usage; and report atypical system account usage. Automated mechanisms can include internal system functions and email, telephonic, and text messaging notifications.
Account Management | Automated Temporary and Emergency Account Management
Automatically [Selection: remove; disable] temporary and emergency accounts after [Assignment: organization-defined time period for each type of account].

Management of temporary and emergency accounts includes the removal or disabling of such accounts automatically after a predefined time period rather than at the convenience of the system administrator. Automatic removal or disabling of accounts provides a more consistent implementation.
Disabling expired, inactive, or otherwise anomalous accounts supports the concepts of least privilege and least functionality which reduce the attack surface of the system.
Automatically audit account creation, modification, enabling, disabling, and removal actions.
Account management audit records are defined in accordance with AU-2 and reviewed, analyzed, and reported in accordance with AU-6.
Require that users log out when [Assignment: organization-defined time period of expected inactivity or description of when to log out].

Inactivity logout is behavior- or policy-based and requires users to take physical action to log out when they are expecting inactivity longer than the defined period. Automatic enforcement of inactivity logout is addressed by AC-11.
Implement [Assignment: organization-defined dynamic privilege management capabilities].

In contrast to access control approaches that employ static accounts and predefined user privileges, dynamic access control approaches rely on runtime access control decisions facilitated by dynamic privilege management, such as attribute-based access control. While user identities remain relatively constant over time, user privileges typically change more frequently based on ongoing mission or business requirements and the operational needs of organizations. An example of dynamic privilege management is the immediate revocation of privileges from users as opposed to requiring that users terminate and restart their sessions to reflect changes in privileges. Dynamic privilege management can also include mechanisms that change user privileges based on dynamic rules as opposed to editing specific user profiles. Examples include automatic adjustments of user privileges if they are operating out of their normal work times, if their job function or assignment changes, or if systems are under duress or in emergency situations. Dynamic privilege management includes the effects of privilege changes, for example, when there are changes to encryption keys used for communications.

Privileged roles are organization-defined roles assigned to individuals that allow those individuals to perform certain security-relevant functions that ordinary users are not authorized to perform. Privileged roles include key management, account management, database administration, system and network administration, and web administration. A role-based access scheme organizes permitted system access and privileges into roles. In contrast, an attribute-based access scheme specifies allowed system access and privileges based on attributes.

preview_rows: Assign the Data Protection Officer to ensure that all personal data processing activities comply with the relevant data protection laws and regulations through governing and implementing PDPL provisions and policies.

Provide mechanisms that must be adhered to give a response channel to data subject requests regarding their rights.

Build a dedicated DSR portal or intake form. Define an internal workflow: intake → identity verification → fulfilment → response. Respond within 30 days; extensions up to 30 additional days must be justified and communicated to the data subject in advance.

Notification for personal data amendment to any related parties that process such data, for example, by email.

Maintain a data-sharing register. When data is corrected or updated, trigger notifications to all downstream processors/recipients. Log each notification event with timestamp and recipient for audit purposes.
Procedure for the Competent Authority notification of a privacy breach or event within 72 hours and for the data subject in case of harm.

Create and rehearse a Breach Response Plan. Designate a breach response team. Notify SDAIA within 72 hours of becoming aware of a breach. Notify affected data subjects where harm is likely. Log incident timeline, impact assessment, and all notifications.

sheets.name: PDPL Principles
detected_headers: Entity must take reasonable measures to ensure personal data is accurate and up to date (e.g. by regularly reviewing the data it holds), and must provide individuals with the opportunity to correct and update their personal data where necessary.
preview_rows: PDPL Data Processing Principles (PwC KSA PDPL Series)
Although the PDPL does not explicitly list principles, they are embedded in its provisions. Source: PwC KSA Personal Data Protection Law Series.

Entity must ensure it processes and discloses personal data only after having an appropriate lawful basis; process personal data only in ways that the data subject would reasonably expect; and be open and clear towards data subjects when processing their personal data.

Entity must have a specific purpose for processing personal data, which must be documented in the RoPA; and must only collect and process personal data to fulfil a legitimate purpose specified in the RoPA — not beyond such purpose.
Entity must only collect and process the minimum amount of personal data that is relevant, necessary, and adequate to fulfil the purposes for which it is processed.

Entity must process personal data no longer than is necessary for the purposes for which the personal data has been collected, unless processing (storing) for a longer time is required by applicable laws.

preview_rows: Provide clear and accessible notice of privacy practices to data subjects
A publicly accessible privacy notice describes what personal information is collected, why it is collected, how it is used, shared, and retained, and how individuals can exercise their rights.
Privacy policy on company website (footer link); layered notice at point of collection; annual legal review; GDPR/CCPA compliant.
Privacy notice document with effective date; website screenshot showing accessibility; legal review records
1) Obtain current privacy notice. 2) Verify accessible from website homepage. 3) Review content against required elements (collection, use, sharing, rights). 4) Confirm annual legal review.
Comprehensive privacy notice covering all required GAPP/GDPR/CCPA elements.
Privacy notice with date; legal review sign-off
Layered or just-in-time notice provided when personal information is collected.
Screenshots of collection forms with privacy notice links
Annual review of privacy notice for accuracy and regulatory currency.
Obtain and manage valid consent for personal information processing
A consent management platform captures, stores, and manages consent preferences for personal information processing, with preference center allowing individuals to update choices.
OneTrust CMP for cookie consent; explicit opt-in for marketing; consent records stored with timestamp and version; consent withdrawal honored within 48 hours.
CMP configuration; consent receipt records; preference center screenshots; consent withdrawal process
1) Review consent mechanism design (affirmative opt-in required). 2) Verify consent records captured. 3) Test consent withdrawal process. 4) Confirm pre-checked boxes not used.
CMP captures cookie consent with granular category choices.
CMP configuration; consent banner screenshots; consent log samples
Explicit opt-in recorded for marketing communications with timestamp and consent text version.
Consent database records; opt-in form screenshots
Process to honor consent withdrawal requests within defined timeframe.
Withdrawal request log; processing confirmation records
Collect only personal information necessary for stated purposes
Data minimization principles are applied to all data collection activities; Privacy Impact Assessments (PIAs) verify that only necessary data is collected for new or changed processing.
PIA required for new personal data processing; data minimization review in SDLC; annual review of collected data fields against necessity.
PIA records; data collection justification documents; annual data inventory reviews
1) Review PIA process. 2) Sample 3 recent PIAs – verify data minimization review. 3) Review data fields collected against stated purpose.
PIA conducted for all new or significantly changed personal data processing activities.
PIA records with approval signatures; DPIA for high-risk processing
Annual review of all collected data fields to eliminate unnecessary collection.
Data inventory with minimization review notes; field removal records
